claim: The Silk Road's go-between language survives in one hidden mountain valley.

start.title: Silk
start.description: Fine, lustrous, natural fiber produced by various arthropods

knots.passage: The first evidence of the long distance silk trade is the finding of silk in the hair of an Egyptian mummy of the 21st dynasty, c.1070 BC. The silk trade reached as far as the Indian subcontinent, the Middle East, Europe, and North Africa. This trade was so extensive that the major set of trade routes between Europe and Asia came to be known as the Silk Road.
knots.hatnote: Silk travelled so far that the trade routes were named after it.

knots.passage: In 568, the Byzantine ruler Justin II was greeted by a Sogdian embassy representing Istämi, ruler of the First Turkic Khaganate, who formed an alliance with the Byzantines against Khosrow I of the Sasanian Empire that allowed the Byzantines to bypass the Sasanian merchants and trade directly with the Sogdians for purchasing Chinese silk. Although the Byzantines had already procured silkworm eggs from China by this point, the quality of Chinese silk was still far greater than anything produced in the West, a fact that is perhaps emphasized by the discovery of coins minted by Justin II found in a Chinese tomb of Shanxi province dated to the Sui dynasty (581–618).
knots.hatnote: Byzantium could make silk by then, but still bought China's best from Sogdian traders.

knots.passage: The Samanids occupied the Sogdian region from circa 819 until 999, establishing their capital at Samarkand (819–892) and then at Bukhara (892–999). During this time the Sogdian language gradually declined in favour of the Persian language of the Samanids (the ancestor of the modern Tajik language), the spoken language of renowned poets and intellectuals of the age such as Ferdowsi (940–1020).
knots.hatnote: The Sogdian traders' homeland was later conquered, and Persian took over.

knots.passage: The economic and political importance of Sogdian guaranteed its survival in the first few centuries after the Muslim conquest of Sogdia in the early eighth century. A dialect of Sogdian spoken around the 8th century in Osrushana (capital: Bunjikat, near present-day Istaravshan, Tajikistan), a region to the south of Sogdia, developed into the Yaghnobi language and has survived into the 21st century. It is spoken by the Yaghnobi people.
knots.hatnote: Yet one mountain dialect of Sogdian held on.

knots.passage: The ancient Sogdians fled to the Yaghnob Valley to escape the Abbasid Caliphate. Their direct descendants, the Yaghnobi, lived there in peaceful isolation until the 1820s.
knots.hatnote: Its speakers had climbed out of reach long before.

payoff: Sogdian merchants sold China's silk to Byzantium; when their world fell to Persian, their language hid in a valley and is still spoken.
